**CHAPTER II**

**REVIEW OF LITERATURE AND STUDIES**

This chapter presents the review of related literature and studies relevant to the development of the proposed system, VIGILANT: A Virtual Inspection Gateway with Intelligent Logging and Access Network Traffic Control. The purpose of this chapter is to examine existing concepts, technologies, and previous research related to internet usage behavior, digital distraction, network monitoring systems, and intelligent content filtering. It also discusses studies involving Natural Language Processing, proxy-based traffic interception, and modern network management approaches used to regulate internet access and improve digital well-being. The reviewed literature and studies provide theoretical and technical foundations that support the development of the proposed system and help identify research gaps that this study aims to address.

CONCEPTUAL LITERATURE

The system behind VIGILANT draws on a surprisingly wide range of fields: networking infrastructure, artificial intelligence, and behavioral psychology, none of which normally have much to say to each other. That combination is worth taking seriously. Network gateways, edge computing, context-aware filtering, natural language processing, behavioral monitoring, and the now-familiar phenomenon of doomscrolling all factor into its design, and altogether they sketch an approach to managing internet traffic that is less about restriction and more on nudging people toward their healthier digital habits. That is a harder problem than it really sounds.

Starting with the hardware layer. A network gateway is, at its most basic, a device that sits between a private network and the public network or the internet, routing data, translating protocols, and enforcing security policies. While foundational, these protocols are essential for the chokepoint through where everything passes. Edge computing builds on that positioning by pushing computational work to the network's periphery, rather than offloading it to a distant cloud server. The payoff is twofold: reduced latency because decisions happen in milliseconds, locally and better privacy, because sensitive data doesn't need to travel anywhere. In environments where real-time analysis actually matters, that's not a small thing \[19\]\[20\].

Transparent proxies do much of the heavy lifting in practice. It intercepts and inspects traffic without requiring any changes on the client side, which is why they are very useful for systems that need to monitor without disrupting. A normal user on a household network shouldn't have to configure anything; the analysis happens underneath them. This transparency is essential for VIGILANT, since the whole point is seamless integration into existing setups rather than imposing something clunky device on top of them \[21\]\[22\].

Where things get more interesting is the filtering layer. Traditional content controls are mostly blacklist-driven: block a domain, allow another. Simple, and easily circumvented. Context-aware filtering tries to do something harder, assessing content based on what it actually means rather than just where it came from. So a social media post about historical events might pass through while a feed algorithmically surfacing outrage gets throttled. The distinction requires natural language processing to pull off. NLP, as a branch of AI, gives machines the ability to parse human language, and techniques like named entity recognition can extract meaningful context from webpage text, flagging not just what a page is but what kind of thing it's about \[23\]\[24\]\[25\].

Behavioral monitoring completes the picture. Tracking metrics like request velocity and session duration sounds dry, but the patterns are revealing. Someone who refreshes the same news site forty times in an hour is exhibiting something different from someone who reads an article and moves on. Which, come to think of it, is the whole point: the system isn't trying to make moral judgments about content so much as recognize when a user's behavior suggests they've tipped into compulsive consumption territory \[26\].

That tipping point has a name now: doomscrolling. The term describes the compulsive scrolling through negative or distressing content that social media algorithms have gotten remarkably good at inducing. The system is conceptually grounded in dopamine-driven reward mechanisms that reinforce repetitive digital consumption behaviors, which are approximated through observable network request patterns and mitigated using behavioral throttling. Constant novelty triggers small reward responses; the brain's negativity bias keeps attention hooked on alarming information; and the endless scroll format removes any natural stopping point. The result isn't just wasted time. Studies have linked heavy doomscrolling to cognitive fatigue, shortened attention spans, and heightened anxiety \[27\]\[28\]\[29\]. One widely-cited figure puts the share of U.S. adults who report being online "almost constantly" at over 30 percent; in high-engagement markets like the Philippines, the numbers look similar \[30\].

The foundational literature here spans decades. Kurose and Ross's Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach remains probably the clearest account of how edge devices and gateways fit into network architecture \[31\]. Tanenbaum's Computer Networks covers layered models in depth \[32\], while Stevens's TCP/IP Illustrated gets into the protocol-level details that matter for any system trying to intercept and inspect traffic without breaking things \[33\]. On the NLP side, Jurafsky and Martin's Speech and Language Processing is still the standard reference for the statistical and linguistic machinery behind content analysis \[34\], and Lane et al.'s Natural Language Processing in Action offers the kind of hands-on Python implementation that actually proves the concepts work at small scale \[35\].

The market context is worth noting briefly. The edge computing sector was valued at roughly $23.65 billion in 2024, and projections have it reaching $327.79 billion by 2033, driven by demand from healthcare, education, and industrial IoT \[36\]. Meanwhile, somewhere around 35 percent of people show signs of internet addiction by clinical measures, with doomscrolling implicated as a contributing factor \[37\]. These aren't unrelated trends.

The research gaps, though, are real. Privacy versus security in edge deployments is a live debate: local processing keeps data off cloud servers, but edge devices are physically accessible and vulnerable to tampering in ways that remote servers aren't. Encryption standards for edge environments are still evolving \[38\]. Gartner's 2024 market guide on edge computing platforms flags scalability as a problem for small-scale deployments, where hardware constraints can degrade NLP accuracy enough to make the whole approach impractical \[39\]. There is a legitimate ethical argument against pervasive content surveillance, regardless of intent; NLP models carry biases, and it's not obvious who should decide what counts as "addictive" content \[24\].

There's also no real consensus yet on what effective intervention looks like for doomscrolling specifically. Device-embedded controls are one approach, but the literature on non-intrusive, scalable solutions is thin. Harvard Health's coverage of doomscrolling's mental health effects makes the stakes clear enough but doesn't offer much in the way of standardized metrics for measuring harm or progress \[40\].

VIGILANT's approach is to sidestep some of these debates by keeping analysis local and making throttling responses adaptive and user-facing rather than invisible and absolute. Whether that's the right balance is a fair question. But the underlying bet is that a system which respects privacy and remains legible to the people using it will fare better, over time, than one that simply decides what users should see. That's an opinion built into the architecture, not just the documentation.

RESEARCH LITERATURE

#### *Background on Digital Overconsumption and Doomscrolling*

Digital overconsumption, particularly through social media, has been the focal point in psychological and behavioral research, with doomscrolling emerging as a key maladaptive behavior. Doomscrolling involves the compulsive scrolling through negative content, often leading to emotional distress and reduced productivity. A longitudinal study by \[41\] on adolescents reveals that social media addiction predicts increased doomscrolling over time, using cross-lagged models to demonstrate unidirectional causality, though reverse effects were insignificant. This builds on earlier work linking doomscrolling to personality traits like neuroticism and FOMO, where surveys showed correlations with psychological distress and diminished well-being \[42\]. Considering the potential problem found in this practice, it is timely but chronic relevance for user experiences, political perceptions, well-being, and other outcomes, in validating a self-report measure of doomscrolling. \[43\] concludes in their study that doomscrolling can be considered as a distinct concept that can be closely related to vigilance, problematic use of internet and social media, and fear of missing out.

Further research explores doomscrolling's cognitive effects, such as "brain rot," where excessive exposure erodes critical thinking. A study by \[44\] indicates that the dilemma of the digital age, often referred to as “brain rot”, is associated with negative behaviors, such as doomscrolling, zombie scrolling, and social media addiction, and they are all linked to psychological distress, anxiety, and depression, affecting core functions of the brain like skills, memory, and decision-making. In addition, a scoping review mapped by \[45\] shows that doomscrolling is influenced by a lot of factors, in the study, it includes psychological, cognitive-behavioral, personal, and socio-technological factors, where, also states that decreased mental well-being and increased emotional fatigue is closely influenced by doomscrolling. These studies challenge simplistic views of digital addiction by incorporating multifaceted variables, revealing that while social media offers connectivity, unchecked use fosters pessimism \[46\].

In the Philippines, where social media penetration is among the highest globally, local studies amplify these concerns. Research on Filipino adolescents during the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted doomscrolling's role in digital dissociation, using phenomenological approaches to uncover identity disruptions and attentional fatigue \[47\]. Another study on students' lived experiences of doomscrolling employed thematic analysis, identifying impacts on daily tasks and well-being, and recommended awareness campaigns \[48\]. A survey-based investigation linked excessive social media to depression and poor study habits s showing moderate associations\[49\]. These local findings build upon global research by integrating cultural elements like family dynamics and limited mental health access, challenging universal models and emphasizing region-specific interventions \[50\]. VIGILANT extends this by monitoring behavioral patterns at the network level, using edge computing to detect and throttle repetitive negative content consumption, thus addressing overconsumption proactively rather than reactively.

#### *Existing Network Filtering Systems and Their Limitations*

Traditional network filtering systems, often DNS-based, face scrutiny for inefficiencies and privacy issues. A comparative study evaluated commercial filters like CYBERSitter and Net Nanny, using heuristic testing on popular web searches, and found high over-blocking rates (up to 20%) alongside under-blocking of objectionable content \[51\]. This aligns with research on AI-driven content filtering, where limitations in accuracy and transparency lead to erroneous removals, analyzed through case studies of platform moderation. Methodologies involved dataset bias simulations, revealing that poor training data exacerbates false positives, with conclusions advocating for regulatory oversight \[52\].

Edge computing approaches aim to mitigate these, but challenges persist. An analysis of next-generation firewalls integrated NLP and ensemble learning for malware detection, achieving 95% accuracy in simulations, yet highlighted scalability issues in edge environments \[54\]. Studies on transparent proxies like mitmproxy demonstrated effective traffic interception but noted vulnerabilities in virtualization, using performance metrics to quantify capacity drops \[55\]. These findings challenge earlier optimistic views by exposing practical deployment hurdles, such as latency in decentralized networks \[56\].

Philippine research underscores these limitations in local contexts. A study on ICT infrastructure proposed privacy-preserving frameworks for crowdsourcing, revealing data leakage risks in under-resourced networks through qualitative assessments \[57\]. Another examined online marketplace potential using household surveys, identifying socioeconomic barriers to effective filtering \[58\]. These local works build on global critiques by incorporating structural inequalities, like affordable data plans fueling overconsumption, and advocate for hybrid edge-cloud models \[59\]. VIGILANT addresses these by leveraging local NLP analysis to reduce over-blocking, using spaCy for contextual NER, thus enhancing privacy and accuracy over static systems.

#### *Scalability and Load Testing in Gateway Environments*

The evaluation of network gateway systems under realistic concurrent-user loads is a well-established practice in network engineering research. Early gateway performance studies relied on small pilot configurations of three to five devices, which were sufficient for verifying functional correctness but insufficient for characterizing system behavior under meaningful stress \[90\]. As gateway architectures have matured, particularly those deployed in small office and home office (SOHO) environments, the research community has shifted toward load benchmarks that reflect real-world deployment densities. Contemporary SOHO networks routinely support between 20 and 50 simultaneously connected devices, encompassing smartphones, laptops, smart televisions, and Internet of Things (IoT) appliances. This transition from pilot-scale to SOHO-scale benchmarking has become a de facto standard in performance evaluation literature because it surfaces failure modes, such as memory exhaustion, thread contention, and connection queue overflow, that remain entirely invisible at low device counts \[91\].

Load testing methodologies for gateways are typically structured around two complementary objectives: reliability under sustained load and graceful degradation under peak load. Reliability testing verifies that the system maintains uninterrupted operation—defined by the absence of service crashes, connection resets, or unacceptable latency spikes—over an extended duration with a fixed number of concurrent connections \[92\]. Degradation testing, by contrast, progressively increases the client count until the system reaches a failure threshold, thereby establishing the maximum sustainable operating point. For inline processing gateways that perform deep packet inspection or SSL/TLS interception, these tests are particularly critical because each additional concurrent connection introduces proportional overhead in the decryption, analysis, and re-encryption pipeline \[93\]. Research on software-defined networking appliances has demonstrated that gateways performing application-layer inspection typically experience non-linear performance degradation beyond a connection density threshold, making empirical stress testing at a realistic device count a necessary validation step rather than an optional one \[94\].

The selection of 30 concurrent connected devices as the evaluation benchmark for the VIGILANT system is directly informed by this body of literature. Thirty devices represents a conservative approximation of a dense SOHO or small classroom environment, large enough to surface realistic concurrency-related failure modes while remaining within the operational envelope of commodity edge hardware \[91\]. This figure is consistent with benchmarks cited in evaluations of comparable inline proxy appliances, where 25–35 simultaneous connections have been used as representative SOHO stress conditions \[95\]. Furthermore, the IEEE Network Operations and Management Symposium proceedings have noted that gateway evaluations conducted below 20 devices systematically underestimate CPU and memory utilization, because connection scheduling and context-switching overhead do not become statistically significant at lower densities \[96\]. By conducting reliability and stability tests across 30 concurrent connected devices, the VIGILANT evaluation meets the evidentiary standard required to make defensible claims about real-world deployability in the target environments of households, student dormitories, and small office networks.

It is also worth noting that the hardware environment in which load testing is conducted constitutes a material variable in performance evaluation. Studies comparing gateway performance across memory configurations have consistently found that appliances provisioned with 8 GB of RAM represent a meaningful inflection point: below this threshold, inline inspection gateways are prone to swap-induced latency under concurrent load, while above it, diminishing returns are observed for SOHO-scale deployments \[91\]. Specifying the hardware configuration, and in particular the RAM capacity, alongside the device count benchmark is therefore not merely a methodological formality but a prerequisite for the reproducibility and external validity of any performance claim. This principle is reinforced by the IETF’s benchmarking methodology working group, which stipulates that hardware specifications must be fully disclosed in gateway performance evaluations to enable meaningful cross-study comparison \[109\].

#### *Mechanics of Transparent Interception and Verifiable Transparency*

Transparent proxying is a network interception architecture in which all client traffic is redirected through an intermediary appliance at the kernel or routing layer, without any awareness or manual configuration required on the part of the end-user device \[21\]. In contrast to explicit proxying—where users must specify a proxy IP address and port in their operating system or browser settings—a transparent proxy intercepts TCP and UDP flows by manipulating packet routing rules at the network level. This is typically accomplished using the host operating system’s packet-filtering framework; on Linux-based systems, the Netfilter subsystem and its iptables interface provide the canonical mechanism, through which a PREROUTING chain rule redirects inbound TCP connections on ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) to a locally bound listener process before the packets are forwarded to their original destination \[97\]. The client device observes no modification to its network configuration: it continues to issue requests as though connected directly to the internet, while the gateway silently intercepts, inspects, and re-forwards each connection \[21\], \[22\].

Within the landscape of transparent proxy implementations, mitmproxy has emerged as a prominent open-source tool for research and security evaluation purposes \[55\]. mitmproxy operates by establishing itself as an in-path SSL/TLS termination point: for each HTTPS connection intercepted via iptables redirection, the tool dynamically generates a host-specific certificate signed by a locally installed root Certificate Authority (CA), presents this certificate to the client, and simultaneously establishes a separate TLS session with the origin server. This man-in-the-middle architecture enables mitmproxy to fully decrypt, inspect, and re-encrypt HTTPS payloads in a manner that is, from the client’s perspective, behaviorally identical to a direct connection \[97\]. For traffic originating from applications that implement SSL pinning—whereby the application validates the server’s certificate against a hardcoded public key rather than the system trust store—mitmproxy gracefully falls back to Server Name Indication (SNI) metadata extraction, preserving the ability to identify destination domains even when full payload decryption is not possible \[55\]. This dual-mode operation, combining full decryption where feasible with SNI-based identification as a fallback, is a key architectural feature that distinguishes mitmproxy from simpler traffic monitoring tools.

The concept of verifiable transparency is central to evaluating whether a transparent interception system functions as designed. In the literature, transparency is operationalized not merely as the absence of client-side configuration requirements, but as a measurable interception property: a system can be said to achieve verifiable transparency only when it can be empirically demonstrated, through controlled testing, that a quantifiable proportion of all TCP/UDP traffic traversing the gateway is successfully intercepted and processed without any modification to client-side network settings \[98\]. This framing is significant because it shifts the assessment of transparency from a binary architectural claim—“no configuration is required”—to a quantitative performance metric subject to experimental verification. Studies on transparent proxy deployments in enterprise and research network environments have proposed successful interception rate as the appropriate measure of this property, defined as the ratio of successfully intercepted and processed connections to total observed connection attempts over a defined evaluation period \[98\]. This metric provides the empirical basis for distinguishing a correctly configured transparent interception gateway from one that silently fails to intercept a subset of flows due to routing misconfigurations, protocol edge cases, or load-induced drop events.

The importance of verifiable transparency extends beyond technical correctness into the domain of research reproducibility and system trustworthiness. A gateway that intercepts only a fraction of intended traffic introduces systematic bias into any behavioral or content analysis derived from that traffic, because the unintercepted flows are not a random sample but are likely to share structural characteristics—such as the use of non-standard ports, UDP-based transport, or certificate pinning—that make them systematically different from successfully intercepted flows \[98\]. This non-random dropout can distort request-velocity measurements, content classification distributions, and throughput calculations, all of which are core evaluation metrics in the VIGILANT study. Establishing a high and verifiable interception rate is therefore a prerequisite for the validity of all downstream analytical claims, and it is for this reason that the transparent interception layer constitutes the first and foundational specific objective of this research.

#### *Quantitative Metrics for Behavioral Filtering*

The identification of compulsive or high-frequency browsing behaviors within network traffic has historically been approached through qualitative or heuristic methods, such as domain blacklisting or administrator-defined time-of-day rules. However, the limitations of these approaches are well-documented: they lack the resolution to distinguish between users who engage with the same domain for productive versus maladaptive purposes, and they are inherently static, requiring manual recalibration as usage patterns evolve \[51\], \[52\]. Contemporary research in network behavioral analytics has shifted decisively toward quantitative, parameterized frameworks, in which observable traffic metadata is expressed as numerical features that can be compared against statistically derived thresholds \[99\]. This transition mirrors a broader movement in anomaly detection literature, where the replacement of binary rule triggers with continuous, threshold-based metrics has been shown to substantially reduce both false-positive and false-negative detection rates \[99\].\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Request velocity—defined as the count of HTTP or HTTPS requests issued by a single client device per unit of time, typically expressed in requests per minute (RPM)—has emerged as the primary parameterized feature for detecting doomscrolling in network traffic analysis research \[69\], \[100\]. The behavioral logic underlying this metric is straightforward: compulsive scrolling through infinite-feed social media or short-form video platforms generates a characteristic pattern of rapid, repetitive content-fetch requests as the client’s application continuously loads new media items. This pattern is empirically distinguishable from normal browsing behavior because it produces request velocities that are substantially and consistently elevated relative to the per-device session average \[100\]. Network monitoring studies have operationalized this distinction using a percentage-above-average threshold approach: a device is flagged as exhibiting high-frequency browsing behavior when its rolling request velocity exceeds a configurable percentage of its own session baseline—for example, 150 percent of the computed per-session average—sustained over a defined observation window \[100\]. The use of a relative threshold rather than an absolute RPM cutoff is methodologically important because it accounts for inter-device variability in baseline usage patterns; a threshold anchored to each device’s own session average is more robust to heterogeneous network populations than a single fixed value applied uniformly across all devices \[74\].

The parameterization of content-level features follows a parallel logic. Rather than relying on binary keyword presence flags—which yield non-comparable outputs and cannot be meaningfully aggregated or thresholded—quantitative content analysis encodes textual features as normalized numerical values such as keyword frequency counts and named entity occurrence rates per unit of page content \[106\]. These parameterized representations enable direct numerical comparison across content items and across sessions, and they can be subjected to the same threshold-based detection logic as behavioral traffic metadata. When semantic content features are combined with request velocity measurements into a composite behavioral signal, the resulting detection framework bridges the traditional disciplinary gap between network engineering—which operates on packet metadata, connection counts, and throughput metrics—and behavioral data science—which operates on user activity patterns, engagement signals, and content consumption profiles \[106\]. This convergence is not merely conceptually appealing; it is practically necessary for any system that seeks to distinguish compulsive consumption from productive use on the basis of observable network evidence alone, without relying on device-side instrumentation or user self-report.

The use of configurable threshold values as the primary enforcement trigger has important implications for the generalizability and calibrability of behavioral filtering systems. Unlike hard-coded detection rules, configurable thresholds allow administrators to adapt the system’s sensitivity to the specific behavioral norms of their deployment context: a household with young children may warrant a lower velocity threshold for social media content than a shared student workroom where short bursts of social media browsing between study sessions are expected and acceptable \[107\]. Research in adaptive network management has established that threshold configurability is a critical design requirement for behavioral filtering systems intended for deployment across diverse environments, as fixed thresholds calibrated for one population frequently produce unacceptably high false-positive rates when applied to another \[107\]. This finding reinforces the design choice embedded in the VIGILANT architecture, which exposes threshold values as administrator-configurable parameters rather than embedding them as constants in the detection logic. By grounding its behavioral detection in statistically defined averages, percentage-based deviations, and explicitly parameterized feature representations, VIGILANT aligns with the current methodological standard in quantitative behavioral network analysis and provides a transparent, auditable basis for every throttling decision the system makes.

TECHNICAL BACKGROUND

VIGILANT is an intelligent network sentry that uses Deep Packet Inspection to examine the content of online traffic, and, in contrast to using firewalls, it uses application-layer proxy engine with network-layer packet redirection to block traffic instead of just blocking the packets based on the IP address\[21\].

Transparent Proxying is used by the system’s primary module where end-user devices can connect to the network without requiring manual configuration to their IP addresses and proxy configuration. The researchers achieve this through utilizing linux kernel’s iptables (Netfilter), to intercept incoming traffic and then directing it to another port using port forwarding. This guarantees that HTTP, HTTPS, and Web Socket Traffics are forced onto the connection\[55\]. While VIGILANT operates as a transparent proxy to minimize network reconfiguration, it utilizes a Root Certificate Authority (CA) approach for HTTPS inspection. This requires a one-time installation of the gateway’s security certificate on client devices to ensure encrypted traffic can be analyzed without triggering browser security warnings.

The first module is the network interception layer. When a user tries to connect to the internet, they would send a request through either HTTP or HTTPS, which corresponds to ports 80 and 443, and that would be redirected to the local proxy listener, which is port 8080. SSL/TLS Man-in-the-Middle (MITM): Since modern web traffic uses Transport Layer Security (TLS), to provide a secure connection over a computer network, the MITM works as a Certificate Authority (CA), so that it can be able to decrypt those incoming traffic, analyze their contents, then encrypt and redirect to the destination \[102\]\[55\].

Then the next module is the Natural Language Processing (NLP) Filtering. Once traffic is decrypted, VIGILANT analyzes the content of the web pages. This is where the "intelligence" is applied. Rather than relying on simple and easily bypassed keyword blocklists, the system used the spaCy framework. Through pipeline processing the system will be employing a language-processing that performs tokenization and entity recognition. The engine then scans the tokenized data for specific linguistic patterns associated with unwanted content and if a threshold of prohibited content is detected, the proxy terminates the connection and returns a custom 403 Forbidden page \[104\]\[23\]\[24\].

For the VIGILANT to function as a standalone appliance, the gateway will manage its own network stack. Using hostapd (Host Access Point Daemon), the hardware broadcasts its own secure Wi-Fi signal. Dnsmasq then provides dynamic IP allocation (DHCP) and handles DNS resolution for connected clients, ensuring all traffic is routed through the proxy gateway. Additionally, a Python-based Flask web application acts as the control plane. This interface interacts with the Linux system services, allowing administrators to toggle the protection engine, view real-time logs of blocked content, and manage the system’s SSL certificate installation.

THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK

This study is grounded on theories related to network communication, cybersecurity monitoring, and natural language processing. These theories provide the foundation for understanding how network traffic can be intercepted, analyzed, and evaluated in order to detect potential compulsive usage patterns or consuming distracting content. The project integrates principles from the OSI Model, and Natural Language Processing to support the development of the VIGILANT system.

The OSI Model, developed by the International Organization for Standardization, describes how data is transmitted across networks through seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application \[101\]. Each layer is responsible for specific functions that ensure proper communication between devices in a network. This model provides a structured framework for understanding how information travels from a client device to an external server. In the context of this study, the OSI model is important because it identifies the layers where monitoring and inspection can occur without interrupting normal network operations.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. OSI Model \[101\]

VIGILANT utilizes a gateway-based monitoring approach that intercepts web traffic before it reaches the internet. The interception process occurs mainly at the Transport and Application layers of the OSI model, where protocols such as HTTP and HTTPS operate. Through the use of the network interception tool mitmproxy \[102\], the system captures and inspects network requests passing through the gateway. This process allows the system to observe the content and metadata of web communications, which can then be analyzed for indicators of compulsive usage patterns or distracting content.

Another theoretical basis of the study is the concept of Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS), which are widely used in cybersecurity to monitor network traffic for suspicious behavior or known attack patterns. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) operate through a structured, rule-based pipeline first formalized by \[103\]. The framework is built on the hypothesis that security violations manifest as abnormal patterns of system usage, and that such patterns can be detected by continuously monitoring system activity against established behavioral profiles. The IDS pipeline consists of five interconnected stages — from the identification of acting entities, through data collection and behavioral modeling, to anomaly detection and alert generation — as illustrated below.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2. Synthesized IDS Framework based on the principles of Denning \[103\]

As shown in Figure 2, IDS frameworks operate by first identifying subjects (the initiating entities) and objects (the system resources they act upon), then collecting structured audit records for every action performed. These records feed into activity profiles, statistical models built using event counters, interval timers, and resource measures, that characterize what constitutes normal behavior for a given subject. Activity rules then continuously evaluate incoming records against these profiles, and any deviation beyond a defined statistical threshold triggers an anomaly record and subsequent alert to the security officer. This principle supports the monitoring mechanism of VIGILANT, as the system performs continuous observation of network requests and evaluates them for potential compulsive usage signatures. By applying IDS principles, VIGILANT can identify patterns associated with rapid content refreshing and high-velocity engagement rather than traditional malicious payloads.

In addition to network monitoring theories, the study also applies concepts from Natural Language Processing, a field within artificial intelligence that focuses on enabling computers to understand and interpret human language \[34\]. NLP techniques allow systems to analyze textual data, identify linguistic patterns, and extract meaningful information from written content. In this research, NLP techniques are used to examine textual elements found in intercepted web pages and messages. The study utilizes the NLP library spaCy \[104\] to process text data and detect keywords or patterns commonly associated with online contents.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3. Steps of the NLP Pipeline \[104\]

By combining the OSI model, intrusion detection system principles, and natural language processing techniques, this study establishes a theoretical foundation for the development of VIGILANT. The OSI model explains how network communication occurs and where interception can be applied, IDS theory provides the monitoring and detection approach, and NLP techniques enable the analysis of textual content related to unwanted media contents. These theories collectively guide the design and implementation of the system and support the study’s objective of improving cybersecurity awareness and content filtration in network environments.

CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK

Understanding how a proposed system is designed, what theoretical positions it draws from, and how its components interact to produce meaningful outputs is best captured through a conceptual framework. Far from being a mere organizational diagram, a conceptual framework serves as the intellectual map of a study where it communicates, at a glance, the logic that binds the research problem to the proposed solution and, ultimately, to the expected outcomes. Figure 4 presents the VIGILANT Contextual Intelligent Gateway Architecture, a multi-layered conceptual model that illustrates how the VIGILANT system is theorized to operate within the context of unhealthy digital consumption in the Philippines. The framework is not a simplification, but it is a deliberate representation of the system's architecture, built to show not only what VIGILANT does, but why it is designed the way it is, and how each of its operational layers corresponds to a specific research objective. Read from the theoretical foundations at the top-left, through the central processing pipeline, and down to the anticipated societal output, the diagram tells a coherent story: that a context-aware, edge-deployed gateway, grounded in established principles of Natural Language Processing, behavioral science, and edge computing, can meaningfully address the growing digital wellness crisis that Filipinos, particularly students and young professionals, increasingly face.

![](data:image/png;base64,)Figure 4. The VIGILANT Contextual Intelligent Gateway Architecture (Conceptual Framework of the Study)

The conceptual framework is anchored on four theoretical and methodological foundations positioned at the upper-left of the diagram, collectively forming the intellectual scaffolding upon which the VIGILANT system rests. The first is edge computing for local, privacy-preserving data processing. Rather than routing user traffic to remote cloud-based servers for analysis, VIGILANT processes all network data locally, at the network's edge. This design choice is not arbitrary. It is rooted in the established principle that edge architectures reduce dependency on external infrastructure while keeping sensitive browsing data within the immediate network environment \[36\]. In a country like the Philippines, where cloud-based filtering tools have raised legitimate concerns about user data being transmitted to third-party servers \[26\], a locally deployed processing model addresses both the technical and ethical dimensions of the problem.

The second foundational element is Natural Language Processing (NLP) with Named Entity Recognition (NER). It is a well-established branch of artificial intelligence concerned with enabling machines to understand, interpret, and act upon human language \[35\]. Traditional DNS-based filtering systems, as extensively discussed in the background of this study, operate at the domain level: they block or allow entire websites based on their URL, with no understanding of the actual content being accessed \[51\], \[52\]. NLP, and NER in particular, enables a fundamentally different approach. By analyzing the textual content of web pages and classifying named entities including topics, organizations, events, and other contextual markers. The system can distinguish between a student consulting a social media platform for academic group coordination and another user mindlessly scrolling through an algorithmically curated feed of short-form videos for hours on end. This nuanced, semantic understanding is what sets VIGILANT apart from its predecessors, and it is grounded in decades of established NLP research.

The third foundation, Behavioral Nudging Theory, provides the ethical and behavioral science rationale for the system's enforcement mechanism. Rather than hard-blocking content which can feel restrictive, circumvents user autonomy, and often backfires, VIGILANT adopts dynamic bandwidth throttling as a soft intervention. The underlying idea is drawn from nudge theory \[86\], which posits that individuals can be guided toward healthier behaviors through environmental design that makes undesirable behaviors less effortless, without removing the option entirely. When the system detects doomscrolling patterns like rapid, repetitive requests to social media or short-form video platforms over an extended session, it does not cut the connection, instead, it gradually reduces bandwidth, introducing enough friction to nudge the user toward disengagement. This is a considered, human-centered design choice that respects user agency while still fulfilling the system's wellness mandate.

Finally, the framework will be grounded in a Developmental Research Design, which dictates the methodology through which VIGILANT is constructed and validated. This methodological stance is important because it establishes that the study's primary contribution is the creation of a functioning system, one whose value is demonstrated not through hypothesis testing but through verified performance against clearly defined technical benchmarks. The claims made about VIGILANT, specifically that it can retain at least 90% of baseline throughput while performing contextual analysis and that it can accurately detect doomscrolling-associated request patterns, are not theoretical assertions awaiting statistical proof. They are engineering targets, and the research validates them through controlled network simulations, component-level testing, and performance benchmarking conducted across realistic deployment conditions. This approach ensures the research meets the rigor expected of an engineering capstone study while remaining honest about what it is actually building and what it is actually measuring.

Positioned beneath the theoretical foundations box is the Input, the Problem Context panel, which contextualizes the raw conditions under which VIGILANT operates. The input is deceptively simple to describe: raw network traffic generated by client devices connected to the VIGILANT access point, limited to a maximum of five concurrent users in the controlled test environment. However, what makes this input particularly complex is its variety. Traffic may be transmitted over HTTP, HTTPS, or WebSocket protocols, each requiring a different interception strategy. For applications employing SSL Pinning—like Instagram, TikTok—where full decryption is bypassed to maintain app integrity, VIGILANT leverages SNI metadata. In these cases, the system transitions from deep semantic analysis to domain-based behavioral monitoring and connection throttling\[55\]. This diversity of input types is not incidental; it reflects the actual heterogeneity of modern internet traffic in a Filipino household or small office, where users simultaneously browse web pages, stream short-form videos, and maintain persistent WebSocket connections to messaging platforms.

The problem context itself is anchored in empirical data. Philippines ranked third globally for daily screen time, with users averaging 8 hours and 52 minutes online per day as of 2024 \[27\]. A significant portion of this time is spent on algorithm-driven platforms designed to maximize engagement through variable reward systems and personalized content recommendation loops \[24\]. The resulting behavioral pattern, doomscrolling, or the compulsive and repetitive consumption of emotionally intense or intellectually low-value content \[42\], has been linked to cognitive fatigue \[45\], measurable declines in attention span among university students \[48\], overstimulation of neural pathways, and elevated stress levels \[27\]. These are not simply anecdotal complaints; they represent a documented, measurable public health concern, and they constitute the problem that VIGILANT is designed to address.

The heart of the conceptual framework is the central processing pipeline, a vertically arranged, seven-layer architecture that moves traffic from raw interception to contextual output. Each layer is color-coded and mapped to a specific research objective, making the framework's structure simultaneously descriptive and evaluative.

Layer 1 or the Physical Access Layer. The pipeline begins at the physical access layer, where a transparent access point is established using hostapd on an Ubuntu Server 24.04 machine (Specific Objective 1). The choice to use a transparent access point, rather than a browser-level proxy or a DNS sinkhole, is architecturally significant. It means that client devices connecting to the VIGILANT network require no manual configuration whatsoever: no proxy IP to enter, no certificate to install, no application to download. All TCP and UDP traffic is automatically routed through the gateway. This frictionless deployment model is essential for real-world usability; most end users in a household or small office environment are not technically sophisticated enough to configure proxy settings, and any friction at the onboarding stage would undermine adoption of the system.

Layer 2, which is the Traffic Interception Layer. Once traffic is routed through the gateway, the second layer handles SSL/TLS decryption and content extraction using mitmproxy in conjunction with a locally installed Root Certificate Authority \[102\]. For standard HTTPS traffic, mitmproxy performs a man-in-the-middle decryption by presenting a locally signed certificate to the client allowing the system to inspect the full payload of encrypted web requests which is made possible by the pre-installed root CA. This is the technical mechanism that enables contextual analysis of HTTPS content, which constitutes the overwhelming majority of modern web traffic. For mobile applications that implement SSL pinning and thus resist standard HTTPS interception, the system gracefully degrades to SNI-based analysis, extracting the destination hostname from the TLS handshake without requiring full payload decryption \[55\]. This fallback mechanism ensures that behavioral throttling can still be applied to SSL-pinned apps like Facebook and Instagram, even in the absence of full content inspection. While SSL pinning prevents the inspection of encrypted payloads by validating the server's certificate against a hardcoded copy, the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension remains transmitted in plaintext during the initial TLS handshake, allowing the gateway to identify the destination domain without decrypting the traffic \[105\].

Layer 3, the Semantic Analysis Layer. With decrypted traffic in hand, the system passes web content through the semantic analysis layer, where spaCy's en\_core\_web\_sm model —a lightweight but capable English-language NLP pipeline— performs Named Entity Recognition on the text content of intercepted web pages (Specific Objective 2). The NER process identifies and categorizes contextually significant entities within the content: for instance, whether the content contains references to educational institutions, scientific topics, news events, or, alternatively, celebrity gossip, emotionally charged political commentary, or the kind of content typically associated with distracting social media feeds. Based on the output of this classification process, content is labeled as Educational, Productive, Distracting, or Harmful, a four-class taxonomy that provides significantly more granularity than the binary allow/block logic of traditional DNS filters. The practical significance of this approach is a meaningful reduction in over-blocking: legitimate educational resources that happen to be hosted on a platform like YouTube will not be indiscriminately blocked, because the semantic classifier can distinguish between a student watching a documentary and a user lost in an infinite scroll of entertainment content \[71\].

Behavioral Analysis Layer is in layer 4. Running in parallel with semantic analysis is the behavioral analysis layer, which operates on network metadata rather than content (Specific Objective 3). A request-velocity monitor tracks the rate at which a given client device sends HTTP/HTTPS requests per minute; abnormally high request rates on social media or short-form video domains are a reliable behavioral signature of doomscrolling, where the client device continually loads new content as the user scrolls. The layer also monitors session duration and tracks repetitive consumption patterns —for example, a client that has maintained an active WebSocket connection to a short-form video platform for more than thirty continuous minutes. The combination of velocity-based and pattern-based behavioral signals provides a more robust detection mechanism than either metric alone: a high request rate during a brief session may indicate legitimate use, whereas sustained high-velocity engagement over a long session is far more likely to represent compulsive scrolling behavior.

Layer 5 is the Enforcement Layer. The outputs of the semantic and behavioral analysis layers converge in the enforcement layer, where VIGILANT makes its traffic management decisions (Specific Objective 3). The key enforcement mechanism is dynamic bandwidth throttling, a gradual reduction in allocated network speed that introduces friction without severing the connection entirely. The degree of throttling is determined by a composite score derived from both the semantic classification and the behavioral analysis: content classified as Distracting or Harmful, combined with behavioral signals of compulsive consumption, triggers a more aggressive throttle, while ambiguous cases may simply be logged for administrative review. Other enforcement outcomes include allowing traffic without modification, logging for audit purposes, or applying partial restrictions. The system is engineered with a target response window of sub-50-milliseconds for the classification pipeline. This efficiency is pursued through the use of lightweight NLP models (spaCy en\_core\_web\_sm) and localized edge processing to minimize backhaul latency, a claim that Specific Objective 4 is designed to empirically validate.

Monitoring and Management, it is the sixth layer that provides administrative visibility into the system's operations through a Flask-based responsive web dashboard (Specific Objective 5). The dashboard serves multiple functions simultaneously: it provides real-time visualization of network activity across connected devices, displays session-level behavioral and classification data, enables administrators to remotely adjust the system's filtering strictness and behavioral thresholds, and maintains a comprehensive audit trail of all filtering decisions. The intelligent logging component is particularly important from a transparency standpoint: it ensures that every throttling or blocking decision is recorded with sufficient detail to be reviewed, challenged, or refined by an administrator. This accountability layer distinguishes VIGILANT from blunt, opaque DNS filters that provide no insight into why a particular resource was restricted \[51\].

The last layer is the Performance Evaluation Layer. This layer is devoted to empirical performance evaluation (Specific Objective 4). Because the VIGILANT system necessarily introduces processing overhead into the network path, content must be decrypted, analyzed, and re-encrypted before being forwarded to the client, where there is an inherent tension between analytical depth and network performance. The performance evaluation layer is where this tension is formally examined. Throughput, measured in megabits per second (Mbps), and latency, measured in milliseconds (ms), are the primary evaluation metrics. The target is for VIGILANT to retain at least 90% of baseline throughput. Controlled stress tests using up to five simultaneous client devices will generate the empirical data needed to assess whether this target is met, with results subjected to appropriate statistical analysis.

A particularly important structural element of the conceptual framework is the dashed orange feedback loop that connects the Monitoring and Management Layer back to both the Behavioral Analysis and Semantic Analysis layers. This loop represents the adaptive learning mechanism that distinguishes VIGILANT from static, rule-based systems. As the dashboard accumulates logging data, patterns of user behavior, records of throttling decisions, administrator adjustments to thresholds, this information can be used to refine the behavioral detection logic and, in future iterations of the system, to re-tune the NLP classification parameters. While the present study scope focuses on a fixed-configuration implementation, the feedback loop is included in the conceptual framework to signal the theoretical scalability of the architecture: VIGILANT is not conceived as a finished product but as an adaptive platform, one whose effectiveness should improve over time as it accumulates behavioral data and as administrators calibrate its responses to the specific context of their deployment environment.

To the right of the central pipeline, the framework situates VIGILANT within the broader landscape of existing network management approaches through a side-by-side comparison with traditional DNS filtering. This comparative element is not merely decorative, it is a statement of research motivation. Traditional DNS-based filters, as the literature abundantly documents \[51\], \[52\], operate exclusively at the domain level: they block or allow entire domains without any understanding of the content being served. This leads to two well-documented failure modes. The first is over-blocking: legitimate educational or professional resources hosted on a blocked domain are made inaccessible, creating friction for users who have genuine, productive reasons to access them. The second is under-blocking: technically proficient users can trivially bypass DNS-based restrictions using VPN services or alternative DNS resolvers \[59\]. VIGILANT addresses both failure modes simultaneously, by performing semantic and behavioral analysis at the traffic level rather than the domain level, it achieves greater granularity, and by operating as a transparent access point at Layer 2 of the network stack, it eliminates the VPN bypass avenue that renders DNS filtering ineffective. Furthermore, because all processing is performed locally, VIGILANT avoids the privacy concern inherent in cloud-based filtering systems, where user browsing data is transmitted to external servers for analysis \[26\].

The framework culminates in the expected output: a Healthier Digital Environment. This output is not merely technical in character, it is fundamentally human. The anticipated outcomes include the mitigation of doomscrolling and its associated cognitive effects, such as short-form content-induced attention deficit and attentional fatigue \[44\], \[45\]; the promotion of sustained productivity and cognitive focus among users in the deployment environment; and the preservation of user privacy through the system's edge-only, cloud-independent architecture. The intended beneficiaries are explicitly identified as households, students, and small office settings, low-density network environments of up to five devices, which are precisely the contexts in which digital wellness interventions are most needed and most feasible to implement. By framing the output in wellness terms rather than purely technical performance metrics, the conceptual framework signals that VIGILANT is not merely a network engineering exercise but a contribution to an ongoing, interdisciplinary conversation about the human costs of excessive digital consumption and the technological interventions that may help address them.

Taken as a whole, Figure 4 presents a coherent, theoretically grounded, and technically specific roadmap for the VIGILANT study. Each element of the diagram, from the theoretical foundations that justify the design choices, through the layered processing pipeline that operationalizes them, to the feedback loop that acknowledges the system's adaptive potential and the comparative panel that situates it relative to existing approaches, serving a deliberate purpose. The framework does not merely describe what will be built; it argues, visually and analytically, for why this particular architecture, operating on these particular principles, represents a meaningful and achievable response to the documented problem of digital overconsumption in the Philippine context.

SYNTHESIS

  The reviewed literature and studies establish that the problem VIGILANT addresses is both timely and interdisciplinary, situated at the intersection of digital behavior, network security, and intelligent computing. The conceptual literature confirms that network gateways, edge computing, transparent proxying, and Natural Language Processing together provide the technical basis for a system capable of inspecting and managing internet traffic locally and in real time \[19\]–\[22\], \[31\]–\[35\]. At the same time, the research literature consistently shows that doomscrolling, compulsive media consumption, and excessive social media exposure are associated with reduced well-being, shortened attention span, emotional fatigue, and lower productivity, especially among students and young users \[41\]–\[50\], \[69\], \[75\]–\[85\]. These findings collectively suggest that internet overuse is no longer simply a behavioral issue but one that can also be meaningfully addressed through carefully designed network-level interventions.

A clear pattern across the reviewed studies is that existing filtering and monitoring tools remain limited in one of two ways: they are either too rigid or too shallow. Traditional DNS-based and blacklist-driven filters are useful for basic restriction, but they lack semantic awareness and frequently result in over-blocking, under-blocking, and easy circumvention \[51\]–\[59\]. On the other hand, recent advances in NLP and content-aware analysis demonstrate that language-based classification can substantially improve filtering accuracy by examining the actual meaning and context of content rather than relying only on domain names or keywords \[23\]–\[25\], \[60\]–\[68\]. Studies on edge computing further support local processing as a practical approach for privacy preservation, low-latency decision-making, and real-time monitoring \[19\], \[20\], \[36\], \[38\], \[39\], \[70\]–\[74\]. Taken together, these bodies of literature point to the value of a unified system that combines local traffic interception, contextual text analysis, and behavioral monitoring into a single architecture.

Another important pattern in the literature is the growing recognition that problematic internet use should not be addressed through hard blocking alone. Behavioral studies emphasize that excessive digital consumption is driven by emotional triggers, reward mechanisms, and repetitive habits \[26\], \[27\], \[41\]–\[46\], \[69\]. This creates a fundamental contradiction in many existing systems: while they aim to protect users, they rely on absolute restrictions that ignore user context, autonomy, and intent \[51\], \[52\], \[58\]. In contrast, the theoretical and conceptual foundations of this study support a more adaptive and human-centered response. By grounding the system in the OSI Model \[101\], intrusion detection principles \[103\], NLP \[34\], \[104\], edge computing \[19\], \[20\], \[36\], and behavioral nudging theory \[86\], VIGILANT is designed not simply to deny access, but to inspect, classify, log, and respond proportionately to traffic patterns that suggest compulsive or unproductive consumption. This makes the proposed system more responsive to actual user behavior than conventional filtering tools.

The literature also reveals several research gaps that justify the development of VIGILANT. First, there is limited research on systems that specifically address doomscrolling at the network level, particularly through real-time inspection and adaptive traffic control \[40\], \[69\]. Second, although many studies discuss content filtering, network security, or productivity loss separately, few integrate semantic analysis and behavioral indicators within a single gateway-based solution \[54\]–\[56\], \[71\]. Third, local studies in the Philippine context confirm the seriousness of excessive screen time and social media dependency, yet interventions remain largely awareness-based, survey-based, or app-dependent rather than infrastructure-based \[47\]–\[50\], \[75\]–\[77\], \[80\]–\[85\]. This means there is still a lack of practical, deployable systems that can operate transparently within households, student environments, and small office networks. VIGILANT responds directly to these gaps by proposing a privacy-aware, edge-based gateway that performs traffic interception, intelligent logging, contextual filtering, and dynamic bandwidth control without requiring direct user-side configuration.

Overall, the reviewed literature, technical background, and theoretical and conceptual frameworks converge on one central insight: effective digital well-being interventions must go beyond static website blocking and move toward context-aware, behavior-sensitive, and locally deployable systems. VIGILANT contributes to this direction by combining transparent proxying \[21\], \[22\], \[55\], \[102\], \[105\], NLP-based semantic analysis \[23\]–\[25\], \[60\]–\[68\], \[104\], behavioral monitoring \[26\], \[69\]–\[74\], and adaptive enforcement \[86\] into one integrated architecture. In doing so, the study does not only apply existing theories from networking and artificial intelligence, but also extends them into a practical solution for regulating unhealthy internet consumption in small-scale network environments. Therefore, this research contributes new insight by showing how an intelligent gateway can serve not only as a security and monitoring tool, but also as a digital wellness intervention designed for the realities of contemporary internet use in the Philippine context.
